title: WHY DID JESUS SAY TO LOVE YOUR ENEMIES?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS SAY TO LOVE YOUR ENEMIES?
The Command That Feels Impossible… Until You Understand the Cross
There are verses that comfort us.
There are verses that encourage us.
And then there are verses that stop us in our tracks.

Verses that confront our pride.
Our wounds.
Our desire for revenge.
Our secret wish to see certain people suffer for what they did.
Few teachings of Jesus cut deeper than these words:

"But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you."
(Matthew 5:44)
For many people, this may be the most difficult command in the entire Bible.
Love your enemies?
The person who betrayed you?
The family member who abandoned you?
The spouse who shattered your trust?
The friend who spread lies about you?
The person who took advantage of your kindness?
Surely Jesus could not mean that literally.
But He did.
And the reason He did may reveal one of the greatest mysteries of the Gospel.
Because Jesus was not merely teaching us how to treat our enemies.
He was revealing how God treated us.
The Day the Crowd Wanted Blood
Imagine standing in first-century Judea.
Dust fills the air.
The Roman Empire rules with an iron fist.
Religious leaders compete for power.
Hatred divides groups into camps.

People despise tax collectors.
Zealots despise Romans.
Pharisees despise sinners.
Samaritans and Jews avoid one another.
The world Jesus entered was not very different from ours.

Political division.
Religious hostility.
Cultural hatred.
Personal grudges.
And into that atmosphere Jesus spoke words no one expected.
The Greek text records His command as:

"ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν"
(agapate tous echthrous humōn)
Literally:
"Love your enemies."
The word used is not emotional affection.
It is not romance.
It is not friendship.
It is the Greek word "ἀγαπάω" (agapaō).
A deliberate, sacrificial, covenantal love.
A love that chooses the good of another regardless of personal cost.
Jesus was not commanding feelings.
He was commanding actions flowing from transformed hearts.
That changes everything.
Because many believers spend years feeling guilty for not having warm emotions toward those who hurt them.
Jesus never said you must feel affection.
He said you must choose love.
The Difference Changes Lives.
The Ancient Roots Hidden in Hebrew Scripture
To understand Jesus' command, we must go back hundreds of years.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal a God whose mercy extends beyond human expectations.
One of the most powerful Hebrew words is:

חֶסֶד
(chesed)
Often translated as:

"Lovingkindness"
"Mercy"
"Steadfast love"
"Covenant faithfulness"
No English word fully captures it.
Chesed is God's faithful love toward people who often fail Him.
It is love that remains when justice alone would walk away.
This divine pattern appears throughout the Old Testament.
God continually pursues rebellious people.
He calls wandering nations back.
He forgives repeated failures.
He extends mercy where punishment seems deserved.
Jesus was not introducing a new God.
He was revealing the heart of the same God.
The God of chesed.
The God who keeps loving people who keep running.
The Problem We Never Notice
Most people read Matthew 5 assuming they are the righteous victims.
We picture ourselves loving difficult people.
We imagine ourselves extending grace.
But Scripture forces a painful realization.
Before we had earthly enemies...
We were enemies of God.
The Apostle Paul writes:
(Romans 5:8)
A few verses later:

"For if when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of His Son..."
(Romans 5:10)
Read that again.
Enemies.
Not strangers.
Not neutral observers.
Enemies.
The Gospel begins with a shocking truth:
The greatest enemy God ever loved was humanity itself.
Including you.
Including me.
Before we loved Him.
Before we obeyed Him.
Before we sought Him.
Christ moved toward us.
Not away from us.
The Cross Changes Everything
The command to love enemies cannot be separated from Calvary.
At the crucifixion, Jesus experienced betrayal, mockery, false accusations, torture, abandonment, humiliation, and execution.
If anyone ever had the right to seek vengeance, it was Him.
The crowds mocked Him.
The soldiers beat Him.
The religious leaders celebrated His suffering.
Yet from the cross He prayed:

"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
(Luke 23:34)
This was not weakness.
This was divine strength.
The Aramaic language spoken by Jesus contains a rich concept behind forgiveness.
The idea is not pretending evil never happened.
It is releasing the right to personally repay evil.
That is exactly what Jesus modeled.
He entrusted justice to God while extending mercy to sinners.
This is why Christian forgiveness is not denial.
It is surrender.
It is saying:

"God, I trust You to judge rightly.
I refuse to become what wounded me."
That is supernatural.
And that is why the world struggles to understand it.
Loving Enemies Does Not Mean What Many Think
Biblical love is often misunderstood.
Loving enemies does not mean approving sin.
It does not mean enabling abuse.
It does not mean remaining in dangerous situations.
It does not mean abandoning wisdom.
It does not mean removing healthy boundaries.
Jesus loved people perfectly.
Yet He still confronted evil.
He rebuked hypocrisy.
He exposed corruption.
He challenged falsehood.
Love and truth were never enemies in His ministry.
Real biblical love speaks truth without hatred.
Offers mercy without surrendering righteousness.
Extends grace without compromising holiness.
The Freedom Hidden Inside Forgiveness
Many people believe forgiveness benefits the offender.
Sometimes it does.
But often the first person liberated is the one doing the forgiving.
Bitterness feels powerful at first.
It feels like justice.
It feels like protection.
Yet over time it becomes a prison.
The person who hurt you may move on.
But bitterness stays behind.
Living rent-free in your heart.
Stealing peace.
Stealing joy.
Stealing worship.
Jesus commands enemy-love because He knows what unforgiveness becomes.
A chain.
A cage.
A slow spiritual death.
Love breaks the chain.
Not because evil was acceptable.
But because Christ is greater than the evil done against us.
The Most Convicting Question
Imagine standing beneath the cross.
Looking at Jesus.

Bruised.
Bleeding.
Rejected.
And then hearing Him pray for His killers.
Now ask yourself:
Who is your enemy?
Who still occupies space in your heart?
Whose name immediately triggers anger?
Whose face still awakens old wounds?
Now ask something harder.
If Jesus loved His enemies enough to die for them...
Can we continue refusing to pray for ours?
The question is uncomfortable because it exposes something deep.
The Gospel is never merely about receiving grace.
It is about becoming people who extend it.
Why Jesus Really Said It
Jesus told us to love our enemies because that is exactly what God did.
The command is not random.
It is not unrealistic.
It is not detached from reality.
It is the very center of the Gospel.
We love because He first loved us.
We forgive because we were forgiven.
We extend mercy because mercy was extended to us.
The cross is not merely the place where sinners were saved.
It is the place where enemies became family.
And perhaps the greatest evidence that Jesus truly lives in us is not how we treat those who love us.
It is how we respond to those who do not.
Maybe that person who hurt you does not deserve your forgiveness.
Neither did we.
Yet Christ opened His arms anyway.
And that changes everything.
Be honest. This hit harder than many expected.
One day you may discover that the person God used to heal your heart was the very person you once struggled to forgive.
